# Understanding and Calculating Pooled Standard Deviation {#sec-pooled-standard-deviation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Compute the sample-size-weighted pooled SD from a reference study.
- Distinguish a pooled SD assumption from unequal group SDs.
:::

## The idea

When the study design supports a common within-group SD, reference-study group SDs can be combined by degrees-of-freedom weighting: $s_p=\sqrt{[(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2]/(n_1+n_2-2)}$. These reference counts are used to estimate variability; they are not the allocation targets for a future trial.

## When and how to apply it

An explicitly reported pooled SD can be entered directly if its definition and context are appropriate. Pooling two markedly different SDs may conceal variance heterogeneity. If a planned method allows separate variances, entering the two SDs may be preferable.

## Formula at a glance

$$
s_p=\sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A reference study reports $s_1=15$, $n_1=50$, $s_2=20$, $n_2=100$. Degree-of-freedom weighting gives a pooled SD of approximately **18.495** units.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Calculation logic

The example uses the stated planning assumptions and mathematical approximation. Explain why they apply before reporting the numerical result.

### Copy-and-run R

```r
n1 <- 50; n2 <- 100; s1 <- 15; s2 <- 20
sqrt(((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2)/(n1+n2-2))
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
The arithmetic mean of 15 and 20 is not the correctly weighted pooled SD.
:::

## Key message

Pooled SD is degrees-of-freedom weighted, and pooling is an assumption rather than a fact.
